newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Business groups knock Singapore budget.
newsitem.headline: Business groups knock Singapore budget.

text.p: Business groups in Singapore said on Saturday they were critical of Singapore's budget for 1997/98.

"The Singapore Confederation of Industries (SCI) is very disappointed that the budget did not address business call for a pro-business budget to improve our competitiveness in the current difficult environment," the group's president Robert Chua told Singapore newspapers.
Analysts had not expected any surprises in Friday's budget and viewed it more as an interim budget after it had been deferred from its usual February date due to the general elections in January.
But they did favour pro-business measures, such as a cut in corporate tax rates, to inject vigour into the slowing Singapore economy.
The growth rate of the state economy has slowed down to five to seven percent after years of double digit expansion.

In a "Shenton Way budget" favouring the financial sector, Finance Minister Richard Hu handed out several incentives for big league fund managers to use Singapore as their regional base, but left corporate tax rates unchanged at 26 percent.

"The Chamber is disappointed the medium term target of 25 percent corporate tax rate has not yet been implemented even though budget surpluses continue to be substantial," the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry said in a statement.
Singapore's budget surplus in fiscal 1997 is estimated at S$4.8 billion, Hu said.
"Nothing was done to look at the competitiveness of manufacturing in Singapore," an research analyst at a European broking house said.
"But reducing taxes won't really do anything except increase earnings and margins. But is not the real problem which is the high costs of rentals and labour," he said.
Late on Friday, the Singapore International Chamber of Commerce criticised the removal of a tax exemption on provident fund payments for foreigners.

"The removal of the (Central Provident Fund) tax exemption for foreigners will make it increasingly difficult to attract the high quality foreign talent that is essential for regional HQ operations," the chamber said in a statement.
The net result would be companies increasing salary packages for that pool of talent, adding to operating costs and making the affected companies less competitive.
The chamber also said that while it was pleased Hu recognised business costs needed to be contained, it was somewhat disappointed no new incentives were announced to address the problem areas.

One analyst said, "Singapore is pretty much a developed economy and it can't really do much but look ahead and at the higher value added financial services, and hope to pull away the funds from Hong Kong."
